provenance.note: Cellular Adaptation.pdf (General Pathology, Prof. Amal Damiri)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Adaptation = reversible change in cell size/number/phenotype/metabolism in response to stress.
Hypertrophy = increase in cell SIZE, no change in number; typical of non-dividing cells (heart, nerve, skeletal muscle).
Hyperplasia = increase in cell NUMBER; only in cells capable of division.
Atrophy = shrinkage in cell size, usually reversible if the cause is removed.
Hypoplasia = congenital underdevelopment; aplasia/agenesis = organ wholly or largely absent.
Metaplasia = reversible change from one mature cell type to another mature cell type (same germ layer lineage).
Dysplasia = disordered growth with loss of cellular uniformity and polarity; precancerous.
Barrett's oesophagus: squamous to columnar/intestinal metaplasia from chronic acid reflux; risk pathway is metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma.
BPH is driven by DHT (dihydrotestosterone); treated with alpha-blockers or 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.
Chronic hyperplasia/metaplasia can progress toward neoplasia; hyperplasia itself is not neoplasia (proliferation stays regulated).

deeper.title: Why heart muscle cannot hyperplase
deeper.html:
Cardiomyocytes leave the cell cycle soon after birth, so when the heart must pump against hypertension or a stenotic valve it can only make each cell bigger. Sarcomeres are added in parallel, the wall thickens, and the capillary supply and diastolic filling lag behind. That mismatch is why the lecture says the adapted heart eventually weakens.

Source: the lecture's hypertrophy slides.

deeper.title: Why metaplasia is a warning sign
deeper.html:
Metaplasia is a sensible trade: a tougher epithelium survives acid or smoke. But the reprogrammed stem cells now divide in a hostile environment, and chronic injury keeps them dividing. More divisions in the presence of mutagens means more mutations, which is the road from Barrett's to dysplasia to adenocarcinoma that the lecture maps out.

Source: the lecture's metaplasia and Barrett's oesophagus slides.

figure.caption: From homeostasis to adaptation, injury and death, with the five adaptive patterns. Schematic drawn for this site.

title: Carcinogenesis and the hallmarks of cancer
subject: subj:pathanat

provenance.note: ONCO 2 Carcinogenesis.pdf (General Pathology, Prof. Amal Damiri)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Tumours are monoclonal: expansion of a single genetically damaged cell.
p53 halts the cycle on DNA damage ('guardian of the genome'); RB controls G1→S.
Oncogenes are dominant (gain of function, one allele); tumour suppressors need loss of function.
Direct carcinogens need no activation (alkylating agents); indirect ones need cytochrome P-450 (benzopyrene, β-naphthylamine).
HPV E6 inactivates p53, E7 inactivates RB; HPV 16/18 → cervical carcinoma.
EBV → Burkitt lymphoma (LMP1); HHV8 → Kaposi; HBV → hepatocellular carcinoma; HTLV-1 → T-cell leukaemia; H. pylori → gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
t(8;14) MYC Burkitt; t(14;18) BCL2 follicular lymphoma; t(9;22) BCR-ABL CML; t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 Ewing.
HER2 amplification: 20% of breast cancers, treated with trastuzumab. NMYC amplification: neuroblastoma, poor prognosis.
Seven hallmarks: growth self-sufficiency, insensitivity to inhibitors, evasion of death, immortality (telomerase), angiogenesis (VEGF/HIF-1α), invasion/metastasis, immune evasion.
Invasion steps: E-cadherin loss → MMP proteolysis → altered integrin attachment → migration.
CD8+ cytotoxic T cells are the main antitumour defence; NK cells act without prior sensitisation.
Carcinomas spread mainly by lymphatics; sarcomas by blood; ovarian cancer transcoelomically.
Four stages: local, locoregional, generalisation, metastasis.

deeper.title: Why one mutated allele is enough for an oncogene but not a suppressor
deeper.html:
An oncogene is an accelerator stuck on: one hyperactive copy of KRAS or EGFR keeps signalling regardless of the normal copy, so the mutation behaves as dominant. A suppressor is a brake, and one working copy of RB or TP53 is still enough to stop the cell; both copies must be lost, which is why inherited retinoblastoma needs a germline hit plus a second somatic hit. The lecture's 'gain of function bad' versus 'loss of function bad' summarises this logic.

Source: the lecture's oncogene and tumour suppressor slides.

deeper.title: Why carcinomas take the lymphatic road and sarcomas the blood
deeper.html:
Epithelia sit on a basement membrane that lymphatic capillaries, with their open, valve-less junctions, penetrate easily, so carcinoma cells reach nodes first. Sarcomas grow inside mesenchyme rich in thin-walled venules and directly invade them, so they seed the lungs by blood. The exceptions the lecture names, renal cell and follicular thyroid carcinoma, are epithelial tumours that classically invade veins.

Source: the lecture's routes of metastasis slides.

figure.caption: The multistep process and the hallmarks of cancer. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Damage to oncogenes, suppressors, apoptosis and repair genes
Clonal expansion of one damaged cell
Hallmarks: growth, immortality, angiogenesis, immune evasion

provenance.note: Cell Death.pdf (General Pathology, Prof. Mehdi Karkouri)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Necrosis: membrane disrupted, cell swells and bursts, contents leak, inflammation present, always pathological.
Apoptosis: cell shrinks, membrane intact, apoptotic bodies phagocytosed, no inflammation, often physiological.
Nuclear changes of necrosis: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis.
Coagulative necrosis: infarcts in all solid organs except the brain (brain = liquefactive).
Liquefactive necrosis: bacterial/fungal infections and brain infarcts.
Caseous necrosis: tuberculosis, granuloma border.
Fat necrosis: acute pancreatitis (lipases), breast trauma.
Fibrinoid necrosis: immune complexes + fibrin in vessel walls (polyarteritis nodosa).
Caspases: activators 2, 8, 9, 10; executioners 3, 6, 7.
Intrinsic pathway → caspase 9 (BCL-2 / Bax-Bak balance); extrinsic pathway → caspase 8 (Fas/FasL).
BCL-2 overexpression: follicular lymphoma. p53: G1/S checkpoint, activates Bax when DNA damage is irreparable.

deeper.title: Why brain infarcts liquefy
deeper.html:
The brain has little extracellular collagen to hold a coagulated scaffold together, and its cells are rich in lysosomal enzymes and lipids. After ischaemia, microglia and leukocytes digest the dead tissue completely, leaving a fluid-filled cyst. That is why the lecture lists the brain as the one solid organ whose infarcts are liquefactive rather than coagulative.

Source: the lecture's patterns of necrosis slides.

deeper.title: Why blocking apoptosis can cause cancer without fast growth
deeper.html:
Follicular lymphoma cells do not divide unusually fast. The t(14;18) translocation puts BCL-2 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter, so the cells simply refuse to die. Over years they accumulate, which is why the disease is indolent and why anti-BCL2 drugs, rather than classical antiproliferative chemotherapy, target its root cause.

Source: the lecture's clinical significance slide.

figure.caption: Necrosis versus apoptosis, with the two apoptotic pathways. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: Cell Injury.pdf (General Pathology, Prof. Amal Damiri)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Mild injury is reversible; severe injury is irreversible and leads to cell death.
Ischaemia/hypoxia is the most common cause of cell injury.
Cell injury starts with ATP depletion → pump failure → intracellular calcium overload.
Cardiac muscle is irreversibly injured after >20 min of hypoxia; skeletal muscle tolerates it longer.
Reversible injury: membrane blebs, swollen ER and mitochondria, myelin figures.
Hydropic change is the earliest and commonest form of reversible injury.
Hyaline = glassy eosinophilic proteinaceous material; Mallory bodies (alcohol), Russell bodies (plasma cells), Zenker's degeneration (typhoid).
Epithelial mucin is PAS-positive; connective-tissue (myxoid) mucin is PAS-negative, colloidal-iron positive; both Alcian blue positive.
Fatty change is most common in the liver.
Autolysis (post-mortem self-digestion) is not necrosis or apoptosis.

deeper.title: Why calcium is the executioner
deeper.html:
Healthy cells keep cytoplasmic calcium ten thousand times lower than the outside, using ATP-driven pumps. When ATP runs out, calcium floods in and switches on the enzymes the cell normally keeps locked: phospholipases that dissolve membranes, proteases that cut the cytoskeleton, endonucleases that fragment DNA, and ATPases that waste the last ATP. That is the lecture's 'three reasons too much calcium is bad', and it explains why the mitochondria, already starved, are poisoned as well.

Source: the lecture's pathogenesis slides.

deeper.title: Why the liver gets fatty
deeper.html:
Hepatocytes handle most of the body's fat traffic: they take up fatty acids, oxidise them, or package them into lipoproteins for export. Alcohol, hypoxia, malnutrition and toxins each block one of these steps, so triglyceride accumulates in vacuoles. Because the liver does so much lipid work, it is the organ where fatty change is most common, as the lecture notes.

Source: the lecture's fatty change slide.

figure.caption: Why lack of oxygen injures a cell: the ATP-calcium cascade described in the lecture, and the free-radical pathway. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Mitochondria poisoned, proteins/DNA damaged, enzymes activated

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Four cardinal signs of Celsus: rubor, tumor, calor, dolor; Virchow added loss of function.
Histamine (mast cells, basophils) is the first mediator released: fast (1 min) and brief (10 min).
Pro-inflammatory cytokines: IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6. Anti-inflammatory: IL-4, IL-10, IL-13.
Diapedesis sequence: slowing → margination → rolling/adhesion → passage through the wall → chemotaxis.
Neutrophils predominate at 6–24 h, monocytes replace them at 24–48 h.
Phagocytosis: recognition (opsonins, TLRs) → ingestion (phagosome) → digestion (phagolysosome).
Fever: TNF and IL-1 → prostaglandins in the hypothalamus. Acute-phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, SAA) via IL-6.
Granulation tissue appears 1–4 days after injury; type III collagen first, then type I.
Labile (epithelia, marrow), stable (liver, kidney), permanent (myocardium, neurons) tissues.
Brain repairs by gliosis (astrocytes), not fibroblasts.
Abscess = localised pus cavity; phlegmon = diffuse, streptococcal hyaluronidase; empyema = pus in a natural cavity.
Chronic inflammation: mononuclear cells + fibrosis, months to years, no spontaneous healing.

deeper.title: Why pus is yellow-white and thick
deeper.html:
Pus is mostly dead neutrophils. After they have discharged their granules against bacteria, they die by apoptosis or necrosis, and their DNA, proteases and membrane debris make a viscous, protein-rich fluid. The lecture's 'pyocytes' with pyknotic nuclei are these exhausted cells, and the creamy colour comes from the sheer number of them together with myeloperoxidase.

Source: the lecture's suppurative inflammation slides.

deeper.title: Why streptococcal infections spread as phlegmon rather than abscess
deeper.html:
An abscess forms when the body walls off infection with fibrin and granulation tissue. Streptococci secrete hyaluronidase, which dissolves the hyaluronic acid of the matrix, and streptokinase, which dissolves fibrin. Nothing can contain the infection, so neutrophils and bacteria spread along fascial planes: the diffuse, dangerous picture the lecture calls phlegmon.

Source: the lecture's phlegmon slide.

labels: Repair: granulation tissue, scar or restitution

provenance.note: Introduction to Pathology.pdf (General Pathology, Prof. Amal Damiri)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Pathology studies structural/functional changes in tissues and organs caused by disease.
Only pathologist physicians practise anatomical pathology.
Lesion levels: macroscopic, microscopic-tissue (histology), microscopic-cellular (cytology).
Elementary lesion = one structure affected; lesional complex = several combined.
General pathology = basic mechanisms; systematic pathology = organ-by-organ application.
Aetiology = cause (primary if known, idiopathic if unknown); genetic or acquired.
Pathogenesis = the mechanism linking cause to disease.
Anatomo-clinical correlation is essential for diagnosis.
Rudolf Virchow: father of cellular pathology. Giovanni Morgagni: founded anatomic (organ-based) pathology.
Andreas Vesalius corrected Galen's anatomical errors in De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543).

deeper.title: Why 'idiopathic' is not the end of the story
deeper.html:
Calling a disease idiopathic means the cause is unknown today, not unknowable. Many conditions once labelled idiopathic — peptic ulcer, cervical cancer, Burkitt lymphoma — moved to the 'primary aetiology' column once H. pylori, HPV and EBV were identified. The lecture's own history section shows the pattern: each generation's idiopathic list shrinks as techniques improve.

Source: the lecture's aetiology and history slides.

deeper.title: Why the pathologist needs the clinician
deeper.html:
The lecture insists on the anatomo-clinical correlation because a lesion rarely has one meaning. A granuloma may be tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, a foreign body or a fungus; the age, exposure history and imaging decide. That is why the request form is described as the pathologist's patient interview, and why an incomplete form can lead to a wrong or delayed diagnosis.

Source: the lecture's diagnostic process slides.

figure.caption: The four aspects of a disease process the lecture describes, and how pathology reads them. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: ONCO 1 Intro.pdf (General Pathology, Prof. Amal Damiri)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Tumour = tumour cells + stroma.
Cancer is the 2nd cause of death after cardiovascular disease; lung cancer causes most cancer deaths.
Metastasis is the only indisputable sign of malignancy; benign tumours cannot metastasise.
Benign: encapsulated, well differentiated, few normal mitoses, slow, no relapse. Malignant: infiltrative, mitoses abnormal, necrosis/haemorrhage, relapse, metastasis.
Anaplasia = complete undifferentiation, almost always malignant.
Dysplasia is graded mild, moderate, severe; carcinoma in situ = full-thickness atypia without basement-membrane invasion.
Grading = how abnormal it looks (microscope); staging = how far it has spread (TNM).
TNM: T = primary tumour size, N = regional nodes, M = distant metastases.
Benign = -oma (adenoma, papilloma, lipoma); malignant epithelial = carcinoma; malignant mesenchymal = sarcoma.
Exceptions: melanoma, lymphoma, glioma are malignant.
Teratomas: 95% mature/benign (ovary), 5% immature/malignant (testis).
Blastomas are malignant childhood tumours (Wilms, retinoblastoma, medulloblastoma, hepatoblastoma); chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma are benign.
Desmoid tumour: benign-looking but locally aggressive. Basal cell carcinoma: low-malignancy, locally aggressive.

deeper.title: Why metastasis is the only certain proof
deeper.html:
Every other criterion has exceptions. Some benign tumours grow fast, some malignant ones slowly; some benign tumours lack a capsule and some carcinomas look bland. Only metastasis needs the full malignant toolkit — invasion, survival in vessels, extravasation and growth elsewhere — which a benign clone never acquires. That is why the lecture calls it the one indisputable quality.

Source: the lecture's criteria of malignancy slides.

deeper.title: Why grading and staging answer different questions
deeper.html:
Grade describes the tumour's biology from a slide: how far its cells have drifted from normal and how fast they divide. Stage describes its history in the body: how much ground it has already covered. Two tumours of the same grade can be at very different stages, and treatment usually depends more on stage, which is why the lecture says staging is useful in most tumours while grading helps only in some.

Source: the lecture's grading and staging slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Cytological specimens: cells only. Histological specimens: cells and tissue.
Standard fixative is 10% buffered formalin.
Sections are cut 3 to 5 microns thick on a microtome.
H&E: haematoxylin stains nuclei blue, eosin stains cytoplasm pink.
Congo red stains amyloid, apple-green under polarised light.
PAS stains glycogen and mucin; Perls stains iron/haemosiderin; Von Kossa stains calcification.
Frozen section is fast but lower quality; always confirm on paraffin sections.
Paraffin blocks and slides are archived at least 10 years (lifelong in paediatrics).
IHC detects an antigen with a labelled antibody.
A forensic autopsy is done when death may be a criminal matter; a clinical autopsy finds the medical cause.

deeper.title: Why formalin, and why 10 percent
deeper.html:
Formalin cross-links proteins, which stops autolysis and putrefaction while keeping the shape of cells. Too weak and it fails to penetrate a large specimen before decay begins; too strong and it hardens the tissue and masks antigens. The 10 percent buffered solution is the compromise that also keeps most immunohistochemical epitopes readable, which is why the lecture's clinical case rejects Bouin, saline and 50 percent formalin.

Source: the lecture's fixation and clinical case slides.

deeper.title: Why frozen sections look worse
deeper.html:
Ice crystals form inside cells during freezing and tear the cytoplasm, and the cryostat cuts thicker, less even sections than a microtome on paraffin. The pathologist can still answer yes-or-no questions during surgery — margin clear or not, tumour present or not — but subtle grading and immunostaining wait for the permanent sections.

Source: the lecture's frozen section slides.

figure.caption: The standard histopathology workflow from the operating room to the report. Schematic drawn for this site.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Three vessel layers: intima (endothelium), media (smooth muscle), adventitia (connective tissue, vasa vasorum).
Leukocyte extravasation and vascular leakage occur in post-capillary venules.
Hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out (arteriolar end); oncotic pressure (albumin) pulls it in (venular end).
Transudate: protein <3 g/dL, few cells, clear, SG <1.016, no inflammation. Exudate: protein >3 g/dL, many cells, cloudy, SG >1.020, inflammatory.
Oedema becomes evident when interstitial fluid increases by 2.5–3 L; fluid in a cavity is an effusion.
Five causes of oedema: ↑hydrostatic pressure, ↓oncotic pressure, ↑permeability, lymphatic obstruction, Na/water retention.
Anasarca = generalised oedema.
Pitting oedema: cardiac, renal, hepatic, DVT. Non-pitting: lymphoedema, lipoedema, myxoedema.
Pulmonary oedema: left heart failure, ARDS, high altitude — pink frothy sputum.
Cerebral oedema: narrow sulci, flattened gyri.
Lymphoedema: radical mastectomy, filariasis (elephantiasis).

deeper.title: Why heart failure swells the ankles and cirrhosis swells the belly
deeper.html:
In right heart failure, blood backs up in the veins, raising hydrostatic pressure most where gravity adds to it, so fluid leaks into the ankles first and pits on pressure. In cirrhosis, albumin production falls and portal pressure rises at the same time, so fluid escapes across the peritoneal capillaries into the abdomen as ascites. Same Starling law, different force and different site.

Source: the lecture's hydrostatic and oncotic pressure slides.

deeper.title: Why lymphoedema does not pit
deeper.html:
Lymph carries protein. When lymphatics are blocked, protein accumulates in the interstitium and pulls water with it, and chronic protein-rich fluid stimulates fibroblasts and fat deposition. The tissue becomes firm and thick, so a fingertip no longer leaves a dent — the non-pitting, skin-thickening oedema of filariasis or post-mastectomy arms.

Source: the lecture's lymphatic obstruction and non-pitting oedema slides.

figure.caption: Fluid exchange across the capillary and the five causes of oedema. Schematic drawn for this site.
